the problem

Does 50°F with a breeze mean a T-shirt, or a jacket?

Coming from Texas, I often found it hard to read information from weather apps and translate it into an outfit. Dallas was mostly warm, so I wasn’t used to the cold weather of New England. I was often either underdressed or overdressed, and felt frustrated that I couldn’t get it right.

This pain point was shared by students across Yale. Many from outside the East Coast felt the same frustration, and I thought it would be a fun experience to build a relatable solution we could keep using outside of the course.

I designed and built Fit for the Weather with two classmates for the Full Stack Web Programming course at Yale in 2023. Although the assignment was graded on its technical requirements, I approached it as a product rather than just a web application, and designed it around how people would actually use it.

“Terms like ‘Fool’s Spring’ show how confusing the weather can get here, and I wish I was better prepared.”

problem statement

Students who struggle to dress for the weather need an intuitive way to see which of their clothes work each day, because they want to focus on schoolwork, not their outfits.

how might we…

help students dress for the whole day’s weather using only the clothes they already own?

process

Redesigning a 2023 class project in 2026

In 2023 we built a desktop web app that met a full-stack course’s rubric: a database of closet photos, a front end that chose which ones to show, and a live weather connection. In 2026 I came back to it to make the recommendations more personal and part of the morning. Each step below sets the 2023 version beside what changed.

I started from what students told us in 2023

No existing app connected the weather to the user’s own wardrobe. I interviewed students on campus about how they chose outfits around the weather, and whether they felt “fit for the weather.”

~20students interviewed
Even New Haven locals were often under- or overdressed.

Weather apps gave numbers rather than tangible guidance, so each person had to interpret them, and their interpretations weren’t always accurate.

So the apptranslates the forecast into clothes, not numbers.

Fits needed to account for the entire day.

Weather in New Haven changes frequently throughout the day, regardless of season, so layering became an important feature to implement.

So the appplans for the whole day, with a layer for the coldest hour.

Wardrobes were smaller than apps assume.

Students had more limited wardrobes than typical recommendation apps expect, and wanted recommendations specific to their own closets.

So the apprecommends only from the user’s own closet.

PersonaThe out-of-state first-year

From New Mexico, used to a hotter, drier climate.

Needs

A way to dress well through every season with the clothes they already have, without buying more on top of them.

Worries

That they didn’t come prepared. Home is far away, so getting more clothes is hard.

Attempted solution

Asking student group chats and friends, and looking on social media for ideas.

Why it falls short

It shows what’s missing from their wardrobe, not how to use what’s already in it, so they end up buying new things.

I audited the 2023 app

I went back through what we built and sorted it into what to keep and what to fix.

kept

  • Personalized recommendations from the items each user added, not generic suggestions.
  • Outfits shown as images, so you see how pieces work together.
  • Small guidance, personal touch: short lines covering items the user hadn’t saved but might need.
  • Layering for changeable days, with a nudge when the weather was expected to change.
  • Useful tips like “Don’t forget your umbrella!” on rainy days.

fixed

1
Desktop-friendly, but not mobile

People check the weather on their phones, so a desktop-first layout was a barrier to entry.

2
Weather still shown as numbers

“6.9°C, overcast clouds” at the top left the same translation problem we set out to solve.

I reframed the product around the morning

The question changed from “what should I wear?” to “how does this help me start my day?” Some people don’t want to look at a screen as soon as they wake up, so the recommendation had to reach them another way. I kept our two 2023 principles and added a third.

2023Practical and enjoyable

A key design principle was making the product fun to use, with quirks that add to the experience of building outfits and getting creative with them. Clothes are a form of self-expression, so instead of making the product purely practical, I used it to explore different ways to see and experience outfits, through a more modern style of UI.

2023Reliable

Wardrobe apps use a lot of images, details and data to organize and personalize outfits. While thinking through how the product would be built and used, I looked for ways to build it so people could rely on it every day.

2026NEWDesign for different mornings

Device habits are changing, and people start their day in different ways. Some reach for their phone first; others want a quieter start without a screen. Instead of assuming one routine, the redesign meets people where they are with a glanceable display for a screen-free morning, and the phone for when they want it.

I explored different display options for outfits

I looked at different ways the day’s outfits could reach people, including apps that use physical devices like e-ink readers to get information to people faster, and chose a reader that shows the day’s outfits without a phone. Then I tried arranging the same outfit on the reader in a few ways.

I defined the system

The reader became the main outfit recommendation feature. The web app became the companion for customizing, editing and archiving outfits, with three pages: Today’s Fit, Closet and Archive. Users can open it instantly by tapping their phone on the reader’s NFC tag.

I designed the screens

Each companion screen went from the 2023 desktop version to a phone wireframe, then a Figma design, then the working prototype. Pick a screen to see it change.

the reader’s layout

I laid out the reader as a scrapbook of outfits above a pixel weather band, designed for a color e-ink screen that refreshes slowly. Select a part to see it on the reader.

I planned the hardware

  • DisplayA color e-ink panel, such as E Ink Spectra 6, that holds its image without power.
  • BoardA small Wi-Fi board downloads a new screen every 30 minutes. E-ink only uses power while it redraws, so a battery lasts weeks.
  • ServerBuilds each screen with the forecast, outfit choice and layout.
  • NFC tagA passive sticker on the chin holds the app’s link.
solution

2026 redesign

Try the working prototype with a copy of my closet and today’s weather. The reader cycles through outfits that fit the day, and the phone beside it lets you build and save a fit or add your own clothes. Your changes stay in your browser.

the logic

How the closet reads the weather

Every part of an outfit answers to a different stretch of the day. Tops follow the warmest hour, bottoms the typical hour, and the outer layer the coldest, with a 5° buffer for borderline days. Build a day below and my closet will narrow to what fits.

visual design

Soft blues, hand-drawn objects and color e-ink

The palette balances function with personality through lighter, neutral shades that don’t clash with the colors of the clothes. I used a deep ink blue for text, a sky blue for anything you can tap, and a warm gray background on the color e-ink reader. The navigation uses objects from a closet instead of standard icons, for a touch of humor.

outcome

Recognized, and still worn

Best Project

Voted by classmates. We presented the product along with how it was built, and how it could make our daily lives easier.

Still in use

Fit for the Weather is still used today by peers and by me.

reflection

UX thinking doesn’t wait for a UX assignment

UI/UX thinking isn’t limited to assignments that are explicitly about UI/UX. The skills carry over and enrich products whose main goal is something else, like this project’s original premise as a full-stack course project.

Thinking about users through both a software engineering lens and a user-focused lens helped me balance technical constraints, reality and my ideas for the design. It also gave me practice switching between those ways of thinking to contribute to a high-quality product like Fit for the Weather.
